texts.facts: 2. Present Application is preferred for quashing and setting aside the Criminal Complaint bearing Regular Criminal Case No. 122/2024 arising out of Crime No. 128/2020 and Chargesheet No. 121/2024 dated 2/7/2024 registered with Police Station, Katol, District Nagpur for the offence punishable under Sections 188, 272, 273 and 328 of Indian Penal Code (for short, 'IPC') read with Sections 26(2)(i), 26(2)(iv), 30(2)(a) and 59 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (for short, 'FSS Act'). 3. The prosecution case in brief is that, the Respondent No.2/Complainant, who was the Food Safety Officer, Nagpur, received a phone call from the Police Station, Katol informing that Police Officer has seized four wheeler vehicle bearing registration No. MH-31-CQ-2980 which was carrying contraband articles as declared by the State Government in view of Notification dated 19/7/2019. Accordingly, the contraband articles were seized by the Police after taking search of the vehicle along with panchas. 4. It is further case of the prosecution that after receipt of such 3/12 Judg.APL.252.2020.odt information Complainant along with panchas went to the Police Station, Katol and taken search of the vehicle along with panchas, wherein the Complainant found Gutkha, which is declared as contraband article by the State Government. Thereafter the Complainant has taken the sample of the said contraband article in presence of panchas and sent the same to the Food and Drugs Administrations Laboratory, Nagpur on 30/10/2019. Accordingly, Complainant received the Report of Food Analyst, Food and Drugs Administrations Laboratory, Nagpur dated 7/12/2019, wherein it is mentioned that the sample of Gutkha is a contraband article in view of the Notification dated 19/7/2019 issued by the State Government under Section 30(2) (a) of FSS Act. On the basis of above report, an offence came to be registered against the Applicants. 5. It is the submission of Applicant that Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006 is a separate enactment, and therefore, provisions of IPC is not applicable. It is further stated that under FSS Act an independent procedure for search, seizure, sampling and consent of the Commissioner prior to lodging prosecution are the mandatory requirement, but in violation of the same, offence is registered against them. Hence, same deserves to be [LEAKAGE_MASK] and [LEAKAGE_MASK]. 4/12 Judg.APL.252.2020.odt 6. In support of the submission, Applicants have relied upon the following Judgments. Hence, in the public interest and for proper investigation, the offence under Sections 188, 272, 273 and 328 of IPC are registered against the Applicants. 9. On going through the First Information Report and Chargesheet, it 5/12 Judg.APL.252.2020.odt is clear that main allegation against the present Applicants is that as per the Notification dated 19/7/2019 the State Government has banned the tobacco as well as scented tobacco in the State of Maharashtra. As such, in violation of the said Notification, the Applicants were carrying Panmasala, Gutkha etc. from the State of Madhya Pradesh to State of Maharashtra, and therefore, the offence was registered against the present Applicants.
texts.arguments: Per contra, the learned APP submitted that although the Act of 2006 is a special law and Indian Penal Code is a general law, there is no bar to apply the provisions of Indian Penal Code for deterrent action against the Applicants in order to prevent them from committing further offence. 10. The learned Counsel for Applicants then pointed out from the Notification dated 19/7/2019 that tobacco which was manufactured in the nature of chewing tobacco with additives is defined as "food" under the FSS Act. Therefore, he has made a submission that once it is defined as a "food", it cannot be considered as "an adulterous food or article" in the matter. 11. The perusal of Sections 272, 273 and 328 of IPC indicates that the offence can be made out against the accused where the article involved was food or drink meant to be consumed by live persons and if it is found that the accused has adulterated it and such adulteration rendered it noxious as food or drink and that the accused at the time of such adulteration intended to sell such article as food or drink or knew it to be likely that such article would be sold as a food or drink. However, in the present case, according to the Applicants, ingredients of Sections 272 and 273 of IPC are not satisfied. Therefore, prosecuting the Applicants for such offences is not permissible in the matter. 12. The Applicants further stated that as per Section 328 of IPC, the offence is made out, only in the circumstances, where the prosecution proved that substance in question is a poison, or any stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug etc., and further accused administered the substance to the complainant or caused complainant to take such substance with intent to cause hurt or knowing it to be likely that he was thereby caused hurt or with intent to commit or to facilitate the commission of an offence. However, in the present case, these ingredients are not prima facie established on record after going through the First Information Report as well as Chargesheet. The learned Counsel for Applicants then pointed out the provisions of the Cigarettes and Order Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, supply and Distribution) Act, 2003 (for short, 'the Act of 2003'), whereby the legislature has, in its Statement of Objects and Reasons, held that tobacco is universally regarded as one of the major public health hazards and it is responsible directly or indirectly to the health of the citizens. Therefore, the need for a 7/12 Judg.APL.252.2020.odt comprehensive legislation to prohibit advertising and regulation of production, supply and distribution of cigarettes and tobacco products was recommended by the Parliamentary Committee. Accordingly, for the effective implementation the provisions have been proposed with an objective to reduce the exposure of people to tobacco smoke and to prevent the sale of tobacco products to minors and to protect them from becoming victims of misleading advertisements. As such, it is the submission of the Applicants that by the Act of 2003, Parliament did not totally banned the manufacture of tobacco or scented tobacco products. The provisions of the said Act only prohibits the sale of cigarette and tobacco products to the person below the age of 18 years and by the said Act only the care has to be taken while issuing advertisement for the product of tobacco and cigarette. 14. In the light of this submission, learned Counsel for the Applicants pointed out that the Applicants cannot be prosecuted under the provisions of Indian Penal Code even in a case if it is found that they were carrying the banned articles in violation of Notification issued by the State Government. 15. In support of the submission learned Counsel for Applicants has strongly relied upon the Judgment of Ram Nath (supra), wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the provisions of the Act of 2006 are exhaustive 8/12 Judg.APL.252.2020.odt and substantive for dealing with the offences concerning unsafe food. Section 89 of the Act of 2006 clearly gives overriding effect to the provisions of the Act of 2006 over any other law insofar as the law applies to the aspects of food in the field covered by the Act of 2006. It is also held that the provisions under Section 59 of the Act of 2006 is more stringent than the other provisions. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the case of Sharat Babu Digumarti (supra) also laid down the law that if legislation has enacted certain Act with special provisions having the overriding effect to cover the criminal act, the same will prevail over the general act. In this regard paragraph No.32 of the said Judgment would be relevant to reproduce here, which is as under : "32. Anil S/O Bhimrao Barange And Another vs State Of Mah., Thr. P.S.O. The learned Counsel for Applicants has further relied upon the Judgment of Joseph Kurian Philip Jose (supra), wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that to prove the offence under Section 328 of IPC the prosecution is required to prove that the substance in question was a poison, or any stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug etc., that the accused administered the substance to the complainant or caused the complainant to take such substance with intent to cause hurt or knowing it to be likely that he would thereby cause hurt, or with the intention to commit or facilitate the commission of an offence.
